summary.value: This paper addresses overthinking in large reasoning models by showing that GRPO’s group-relative advantage turns length-penalized but correct rollouts into negative advantages, which misguides learning (Section 3; Figure 1; Table 3). The authors propose Decoupled Reward Policy Optimization (DRPO), which decouples signals for correct and incorrect samples so that length rewards for correct rollouts are normalized only within the positive group (Section 4). Built on a discriminative constrained objective (DisCO; Section 4.1), DRPO integrates an optimized positive-data distribution that maximizes a length reward under a KL regularization and derives a closed-form solution (Eq. 6), enabling efficient on-policy training via importance weighting (Eq. 7). The formulation is general and can incorporate other rewards on positive data beyond length (Section 4.2). Experiments on math reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, OlympiadBench, AIME) and models of 1.5B/7B/8B parameters show substantial length reductions with minimal accuracy loss, consistently outperforming six efficient-reasoning baselines in performance–efficiency trade-offs (Figure 3; Figure 4; Table 1), with training dynamics illustrating controllable length via λ (Figure 2). Additional studies include generalization to logic puzzles (Appendix A.4; Figure 5), ablations on length reward shapes (Appendix A.5; Figure 6), robustness with pass@16 (Figure 7), and qualitative cases showing markedly shorter, less redundant reasoning paths (Figures 8–10).

strengths.value:
1. Clear, convincing diagnosis of GRPO’s failure under composite rewards. Section 3 shows that adding length penalties can flip advantages of correct-but-long rollouts to negative, misguiding learning; this is crisply illustrated in Figure 1 and systematically across diverse reward designs in Appendix A.3 (Table 3). The analysis generalizes beyond GRPO to other REINFORCE-style estimators that couple positives and negatives.

2. Conceptually simple but original decoupling principle. DRPO normalizes length rewards only within the positive group, ensuring verbose correct rollouts receive reduced but never negative signals (Section 4; lines 069–072). This directly removes the identified optimization barrier without introducing heavy machinery.

3. Strong theoretical grounding with a tractable, closed-form construction. The positive-sample distribution P∗ that maximizes the length reward under a KL regularizer is derived in closed form (Eq. (6); proof in Appendix A.1, Eqns. (11)–(12)). This yields a practical weighting scheme for positives computable from on-policy data (Eq. (7)).

4. Principled integration into a discriminative RL objective. Building on DisCO (Section 4.1; Eq. (3)), DRPO cleanly integrates P∗ into a discriminative max–min style objective (Eq. (7)), combining positive-only, length-weighted likelihood maximization with a log-sum-exp over negatives—well-aligned with classical discriminative learning.

5. Stable, implementable training recipe. The method includes a trust-region style KL constraint with a practical penalty relaxation and an explicit algorithm (Algorithm 1), making adoption straightforward. The scoring function sθ and KL estimator are specified in detail.

6. Consistent, state-of-the-art accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across scales. DRPO dominates baselines on 1.5B/7B/8B models in Figure 3, e.g., 7B: reducing average length from 3053 to 1502 (≈51%) with only 2.6% pass@1 loss. DRPO achieves positive AES while baselines are largely negative (Table 1; detailed per-dataset AES in Appendix A.6, Tables 4–6).

7. Controllable efficiency via a single knob. Training dynamics (Figure 2) show λ smoothly trades off length and accuracy: smaller λ dramatically shortens generations (e.g., >50% reduction at λ=0.1) with marginal training-time performance impact, offering practitioners fine-grained control.

8. Difficulty-aware evaluation clarifies where efficiency gains are “free.” Figure 4 decomposes results by benchmark difficulty, showing very large gains with negligible loss on easy tasks (GSM8K: 1.5B, 77.2% length reduction with −1.1% accuracy; 7B, 73.1% with −0.6%), and sensible trends as difficulty increases.

9. Generalization beyond math reasoning. DRPO’s decoupling benefits transfer to logic puzzles (Appendix A.4; Figure 5), achieving a 33.2% length reduction with no accuracy drop (0.972→0.974), indicating the principle is task-agnostic.

10. Robustness across metrics and reward shapes. DRPO maintains superior trade-offs under pass@16 (Figure 7) and works well with multiple length reward forms (linear/concave/cosine in Appendix A.5; Figure 6), with linear rewards offering the broadest operating range.

11. High-quality diagnostic tooling for the community. The paper catalogs prevalent length-reward designs (Appendix A.2/A.3; Table 2) and explicitly demonstrates their failure modes under group-relative advantages (Table 3), providing actionable insight for practitioners debugging overthinking.

12. Persuasive qualitative evidence of reduced redundancy. Case studies (Figures 8–10) show markedly shorter chains with fewer reflection tokens and repeated answers, aligning human-interpretable reasoning behavior with the quantitative gains.

13. Reproducibility and experimental transparency. Training settings, hyperparameter sweeps, generation budgets, and evaluation protocols are detailed (Section 5; Appendix A.2), and a Reproducibility Statement notes code availability in the supplementary materials.

weaknesses.value:
1. Limited novelty relative to existing discriminative RL formulations
- Evidence: The closed-form solution for P∗ (Appendix A.1; Eq. (11)–(12)) is a standard exponential tilting under a KL regularizer, closely paralleling DPO-style derivations (Rafailov et al., 2023) and f-divergence preference optimization (Go et al., 2023). The overall objective extends DisCO (Section 4.1; Eq. (3)) by reweighting positives with exp(rl/λ) normalized within positives (Section 4.2; Eq. (7)).
- Why it matters: The key mechanistic novelty is the decoupling/normalization within the positive set, which could be perceived as a targeted design choice atop known discriminative machinery.
- Actionable: (a) Provide a head-to-head comparison to a simple “positive-only normalization” baseline without the KL-derived P∗ to isolate gains from the exponential reweighting vs. decoupling itself. (b) Clarify theoretical distinctions vs. DisCO/DPO/FDPO, e.g., show that the DRPO gradient cannot be obtained by a straightforward reparameterization of those objectives.

2. No formal guarantees on accuracy preservation or “never-negative” learning signals
- Evidence: The paper argues DRPO “never pushes [correct rollouts] into negative territory” (Section 4, lines 069–072), but offers no formal bound relating λ, the positive/negative class separation, and accuracy retention.
- Why it matters: The central claim is preserving performance while shortening reasoning (Figures 2–4; Table 1). Formal guarantees (even in simplified settings) would strengthen confidence beyond empirical evidence.
- Actionable: Provide propositions bounding the sign and magnitude of positive-sample learning signals under Eq. (7), and, if possible, a toy analysis (bandit or linearized model) showing conditions under which accuracy cannot decrease as λ shrinks within a range.

3. Baseline comparability and tuning may bias conclusions
- Evidence: Some baselines are evaluated using authors’ released models rather than fully controlled retraining (Section 5, Baselines). For trained baselines, hyperparameter sweeps are narrow (e.g., α ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} for RLOO-LP; β ∈ {1e−9, 1e−8, 1e−7} for ALP; w ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1} for HAPO), potentially underexploring accuracy–efficiency trade-offs (Figure 3; Table 1).
- Why it matters: AES is sensitive to the accuracy drop (Table 1; Appendix A.6), and stronger tuning could change rankings.
- Actionable: (a) Retrain all baselines under the same data, steps, generation budget, and decoding (Section 5, Training Details). (b) Expand sweeps (including α/β/w beyond the reported sets) and report best-of-sweep with error bars over multiple seeds (Appendix A.6 currently lacks variance).

4. Compute/latency benefits not quantified
- Evidence: Results emphasize token-length reductions (Figures 2–4; Table 1) but omit wall-clock time, throughput, or energy/FLOPs gains.
- Why it matters: The practical motivation is reducing inference cost and latency (Introduction; lines 044–053).
- Actionable: Report end-to-end latency and throughput gains vs. reference (squares in Figure 3), including variance across prompts and hardware, and normalize by system-level overheads (e.g., verifier calls).

5. Sensitivity to positive-rate sparsity and weight variance unaddressed
- Evidence: DRPO relies on positive-only reweighting ω(o|q) with per-question normalization (Section 4.2; Eq. (7); Algorithm 1). Early in training or on harder datasets (Figure 4, right panels), positives can be rare.
- Why it matters: Rare positives can cause high-variance gradients or degenerate normalization.
- Actionable: (a) Plot positive fraction over steps and stability metrics. (b) Add safeguards (e.g., ω clipping, moving-average denominators, or mixing λ=+∞ updates when |S+q| is small). (c) Ablate these stabilizers to quantify impact.

6. Global λ is coarse; difficulty-aware control left to future work
- Evidence: Figure 4 shows increasing performance cost on harder datasets; the paper itself notes adapting λ by difficulty as future work (lines 509–513).
- Why it matters: A single λ trades off aggressively across tasks of varying difficulty, leaving performance on hard sets exposed.
- Actionable: Implement and evaluate question-conditioned λ (e.g., based on pass rate, verifier confidence, or stepwise perplexity), and show that it preserves the strong GSM8K gains while mitigating drops on OlympiadBench/AIME.

7. Choice and calibration of the length scale C are not analyzed
- Evidence: Length reward uses C as maximum response length (Section 4.2), but sensitivity to C is not reported.
- Why it matters: Miscalibrated C can saturate weights or distort incentives across datasets and models.
- Actionable: Provide sensitivity plots over C (per dataset/model), or learn C adaptively (e.g., from running quantiles of |o|).

8. Limited ablations on DRPO’s own regularizers and scoring temperature
- Evidence: Key training hyperparameters (δ, β0, τ in Algorithm 1/Section 4.2) are fixed without sensitivity studies.
- Why it matters: The KL constraint (δ) and τ in the log-sum-exp for negatives control stability and hardness emphasis.
- Actionable: Ablate δ, β0, and τ to show robustness of the trade-off curves (Figure 3) and AES (Table 1).

9. Generalization beyond math is thin
- Evidence: Only one non-math task is included (logic puzzles; Appendix A.4; Figure 5).
- Why it matters: The claim of a general mechanism for efficient reasoning would be stronger with diverse domains.
- Actionable: Evaluate at least one additional domain (e.g., scientific QA or program synthesis) under the same training/eval protocol to test transferability of the decoupled positive weighting.

10. Lack of a GRPO-style decoupling baseline to isolate the “group-advantage” factor
- Evidence: The paper diagnoses GRPO’s group-relative advantage as the root cause (Section 3; Figure 1; Table 3) but does not show a GRPO variant with positive-only normalization.
- Why it matters: It is unclear how much of DRPO’s gain stems from discriminative training vs. decoupling itself.
- Actionable: Add a “GRPO-PosNorm” baseline that computes advantages normalized within positives, holding other GRPO elements fixed, to attribute gains more precisely.

11. Statistical reporting is minimal
- Evidence: Figures 2–4 and Table 1 present point estimates without confidence intervals; pass@1 is averaged over 16 completions (Section 5, Evaluation) but seed variability is not shown.
- Why it matters: Differences between methods can be within noise for some settings, especially averaged across datasets (Figure 3).
- Actionable: Report mean±std over multiple seeds for key settings and per-dataset confidence intervals, and include significance tests where appropriate.

12. Behavioral analysis is anecdotal
- Evidence: Case studies (Figures 8–10) qualitatively show fewer reflections and repeated answers.
- Why it matters: Quantitative behavioral metrics would generalize the claim that DRPO reduces redundant back-and-forth.
- Actionable: Track reflection-token rates, repetition counts, and premature-final-answer rates across benchmarks, correlating them with accuracy and length to substantiate behavioral mechanisms beyond examples.

questions.value:
1. Clarify novelty relative to DisCO/DPO/FDPO
- Section 4.2 derives P∗ via an exponential tilting under a KL regularizer (Eq. 5–6), akin to DPO-style results (Appendix A.1, Eq. 11–12). Please provide a formal comparison: can DRPO’s gradient (Eq. 7; Algorithm 1, step 9) be reduced to a reparameterization of DisCO/DPO under some choice of rewards, or is it genuinely distinct? A short derivation showing why DisCO with heuristic positive-only normalization cannot recover DRPO’s update would sharpen the conceptual contribution.

2. Formalize the “never-negative” learning signal claim
- The paper states DRPO “never pushes [positive rollouts] into negative territory” (Section 4; lines 069–072), since positives are normalized within S+q. Can you state and prove a proposition that the per-positive gradient contribution is always non-negative under Eq. 7 (accounting for the negative log-sum-exp term over S−q and the KL penalty)? A toy analysis (e.g., linearized model) bounding the net positive term would substantiate the central claim.

3. Robustness when S+q is small or empty
- Algorithm 1 (step 6–9) normalizes by ∑o∈S+q exp(rl/λ). What is the fallback when S+q=∅ or very small (early training or on AIME/OlympiadBench; Figure 4 right panels)? Do you (a) skip the positive term, (b) back off to λ=+∞ (DisCO) for that question, or (c) use a moving-average denominator? Please describe safeguards and their empirical impact.

4. Weight variance and stability of ω(o|q)
- In Eq. 7/Algorithm 1, ω(o|q) ∝ exp(rl/λ) within S+q. Can you report histograms of ω and the positive fraction over steps, to assess variance and stability on hard sets? Were any weight clipping or temperature adjustments applied in practice? This would help interpret convergence behavior in Figure 2.

5. Sensitivity to the length scale C
- Section 4.2 sets rl(o)=1−|o|/C, with C the “maximum response length.” Is C fixed (e.g., the 8k generation budget in Section 5) or question/model-specific? Please provide sensitivity curves for C (per-dataset and model) and discuss how to set/learn C (e.g., running quantiles of |o|) to avoid reward saturation or miscalibration.

6. Difficulty-aware λ
- Figure 4 shows large “free” gains on GSM8K but increasing costs on OlympiadBench/AIME. Since lines 509–513 suggest adapting λ by difficulty, could you add a simple question-conditioned λ (e.g., based on pass rate or verifier confidence) and report its effect on the hard sets, holding easy-set gains?

7. Baseline comparability and tuning scope
- Section 5 (Baselines) mixes retrained models and released checkpoints (L1-MAX, LASER-D, SB). Can you (a) retrain all baselines under the same data/steps/decoding, or (b) at least broaden their sweeps (α/β/w beyond the sets in Section 5/Appendix A.2) and add mean±std over seeds? This would strengthen the comparisons in Figure 3 and AES in Table 1/Appendix A.6.

8. Isolating the decoupling effect
- To attribute gains to decoupling vs. discriminative training, could you add: (a) GRPO-PosNorm: a GRPO variant whose advantage normalizes correct rollouts within positives (keeping other GRPO elements), and (b) DisCO+PosWeight: DisCO with a simple positive-only length weight (no KL-derived P∗)? A head-to-head on Figure 3 would clarify which ingredients matter most.

9. Negative term and τ sensitivity
- The negative part uses τ log-sum-exp over S−q (Eq. 3, Eq. 7; Algorithm 1 step 9). Please ablate τ (and δ, β0 in the KL penalty) to show stability and trade-off robustness. Do smaller τ (less hard-negative focus) mitigate accuracy drops on hard sets in Figure 4?

10. Compute/latency gains beyond token length
- Since the motivation is efficiency (Introduction, lines 044–053), can you report end-to-end latency/throughput/energy vs. the square markers in Figure 3, including verifier overheads? A wall-clock analysis would quantify practical benefits of the 50–77% token reductions (Figure 2; Figure 4).

11. Estimation details for Eq. 7
- The positive weight uses a ratio of expectations estimated from S+q. Is this computed as a ratio of sample means (a biased estimator in general)? If so, what is the observed bias/variance, and did you consider self-normalized importance sampling or control variates? A brief note would clarify estimator accuracy.

12. AES calibration and robustness
- Section 5 uses AES with γ=10 (vs. α=1, β=3) to penalize accuracy drops strongly. Please (a) justify γ=10 and (b) provide a sensitivity table showing that DRPO’s advantage in Table 1/Appendix A.6 persists for other γ (e.g., 5, 7, 12). This will address concerns that rankings hinge on this choice.

13. Additional domains and process rewards
- Appendix A.4 (Figure 5) shows logic puzzles. Since Section 4.2 claims generality to “other rewards on positive data beyond length,” could you include a small experiment mixing a process reward (or verifier-guided step rewards) with rl, to demonstrate extensibility beyond pure length shaping?

14. Statistical reporting and variability
- Figures 2–4 and Table 1 report point estimates. Please add confidence intervals (per-dataset) and seed variance for key points (e.g., λ∈{0.1,0.2}, strongest baselines) and include pass@1/pass@16 side-by-side (Figure 7) to establish statistical significance of trade-off improvements.

15. Implementation details that affect reproducibility
- Algorithm 1 estimates DKL(πold||πθ) (step 8) via sampled tokens. Are there any practical tweaks (e.g., token filtering, EOS handling, KL annealing) that were critical? Also, how sensitive are results to the number of on-policy samples per question (n=8 in Section 5), especially for positive-rate sparsity? A short ablation on n would be helpful.
